mainTopic: פסי ביראות: the allowed gaps between the posts, and אביי's questions to רבה about widening דיומדין, mounds, and reed barriers
overview: This amud continues the laws of פסי ביראות, the boards placed around a well so people may draw water on שבת. It first finishes a ברייתא: for רבי מאיר the gap between the corner posts may be 10 אמות, and for רבי יהודה it may be 13⅓ אמות. The גמרא explains the ברייתא's wording 'like ten,' 'like thirteen,' and 'like fourteen.' רב פפא then shows which well sizes need extra single boards (פשוטין) according to each view. Next, after a סימן (memory aid), אביי asks רבה a series of questions. The first asks whether widening the corner posts (דיומדין) can replace adding single boards, and the wording 'ובלבד שירבה בפסין' shows that it can. The second asks how רבי יהודה closes a gap larger than 13⅓ אמות. The third asks whether a mound can serve as a דיומד, which leads to a dispute over whether we 'picture' (רואין) an object changed once or twice. The last asks whether a barrier of reeds can count as a דיומד. That discussion is given in two versions and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: Ten Cubits or Thirteen to Fourteen Cubits
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends: according to רבי מאיר the gap is 'like ten' אמות, and according to רבי יהודה it is 'like thirteen and like fourteen' אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: …so that they are about ten cubits. This is what רבי מאיר says. רבי יהודה says: about thirteen cubits and about fourteen cubits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא that gives the widest gap allowed between the corner-posts around a well. רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה each turn their cow-based measure into a number of אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each cow takes up about 1⅔ אמות. רבי מאיר allows two teams of three cows: six cows = 10 אמות. רבי יהודה allows two teams of four cows: eight cows = 13⅓ אמות, which is why he gives a number between 13 and 14.

keyTerms.meaning: Corner-posts set up around a public well so people may draw water on שבת
'Like ten', meaning about ten
A cubit, a unit of length

steps.confusionAlert: The numbers are not random. They come from how many cows fit in the gap: six cows for רבי מאיר and eight cows for רבי יהודה, at about 1⅔ אמות per cow.

phrases.english: so that they are approximately ten (cubits),
phrases.notes: Six cows at 1⅔ אמות each come to exactly 10.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
approximately thirteen cubits
phrases.notes: Eight cows at 1⅔ אמות each come to 13⅓ אמות.

phrases.english: and approximately fourteen cubits.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר. רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא that began on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: the gap may be about 10 אמות (six cows). רבי יהודה: about 13 to 14 אמות (eight cows).

steps.title: Why Say 'Like Ten' If It Is Exactly Ten?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר's number is called 'like ten' when six cows come to exactly ten אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Like ten'? But it is exactly ten!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the wording of the ברייתא. If the measure is exactly ten, the word 'like' (about) does not fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Six cows × 1⅔ אמות = exactly 10. Saying 'about' suggests the number is not exact, so the wording seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: But (look), it is…; begins a challenge
They are, they come to

phrases.english: 'Approximately ten'?
But they are exactly ten!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of רבי מאיר's line in the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The math gives exactly 10, so calling it 'about 10' is imprecise.

steps.title: 'Like Ten' Matches the Later Wording
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא said 'like ten' only because it was going to say 'like thirteen' in the next clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he wanted to teach 'like thirteen' in the later clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'like' in רבי מאיר's clause is there for style. It keeps the wording the same as רבי יהודה's clause.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא needed 'like' for רבי יהודה's number, which really is not a whole number. To keep both clauses worded the same way, he also wrote 'like' for רבי מאיר's ten. The word does not mean ten is inexact.

keyTerms.meaning: Because he wanted to teach
The later clause

phrases.english: Because he wanted to teach
in the later clause, 'approximately thirteen.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic matching (wording copied from the next clause)
steps.terutzMaskana: Ten is exact. 'Like' was added only to match 'like thirteen' later.

steps.title: Why Say 'Like Thirteen' If It Is More?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה's number is called 'like thirteen' when it is more than thirteen.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Like thirteen'? But it is more!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now challenges the next number. Eight cows come to 13⅓, which is more than thirteen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'About thirteen' sounds like a little under or close to 13. The real measure is more than 13, so the wording seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: More

phrases.english: 'Approximately thirteen' — but they are more!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the clause that step 3 relied on.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Eight cows = 13⅓, so 13 is too low to describe it.

steps.title: 'Like Thirteen' Matches 'Like Fourteen'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא said 'like thirteen' because it was about to say 'like fourteen.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he wanted to teach 'like fourteen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same kind of answer again. 'Like thirteen' was written so the wording matches 'like fourteen.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer follows the pattern of step 3. One phrase is worded a certain way only because of the phrase that comes after it.

keyTerms.meaning: To teach

phrases.english: Because he wanted to teach 'approximately fourteen.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 4 the same way step 3 answered step 2.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Like thirteen' must mean the measure is at or near 13.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is worded to pair with 'like fourteen.'

steps.title: But It Does Not Reach Fourteen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how 'like fourteen' can be said when 13⅓ does not reach fourteen.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And like fourteen'? But it does not reach that!
steps.whatsHappening: The chain reaches its last link. 'Like fourteen' has no later phrase to explain it, and the real number is below fourteen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now, each word was explained by the next one. The last phrase has nothing after it, so the גמרא needs a real answer.

keyTerms.meaning: But it does not come to that

phrases.english: 'And approximately fourteen' — but it does not come to that!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the clause that step 5 relied on.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 13⅓ is less than 14, and no later clause can explain the wording.

steps.title: רב פפא: More Than Thirteen, Less Than Fourteen
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that the double phrase means a number between 13 and 14.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: More than thirteen, and not reaching fourteen.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains that the two numbers are meant to be read together. They mark the range the measure falls in: above 13 and below 14.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither number alone is precise. Together they describe 13⅓ אמות, so 'like thirteen and like fourteen' is accurate after all.

keyTerms.meaning: More than, in excess of
Reaching

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר's gap is exactly 10 אמות. רבי יהודה's gap is 13⅓ אמות, which is why the ברייתא says 'between 13 and 14.'

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
they are more than thirteen,
and they do not reach fourteen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: יְתֵירוֹת עַל שְׁלֹשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 6 and ends the wording discussion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: the two numbers mark a range
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each number is a separate approximate value.
steps.terutzMaskana: Together they mean 'between 13 and 14,' that is, 13⅓.

steps.title: רב פפא: An Eight-Cubit Well Needs No Extra Boards
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that for a בור that is eight אמות wide, everyone agrees there is no need for single boards (פשוטין).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: For a well that is eight (אמות wide), everyone agrees that we do not need single boards.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives a new ruling: there is a case where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה do not argue at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An 8-אמה well plus 2 אמות on each side for the cows makes 12 אמות. Each corner-post takes up 1 אמה, so the gap between the posts is only 10 אמות. That is allowed even by רבי מאיר, so no single boards (פשוטין) are needed between the posts.

keyTerms.meaning: A cistern or well
Everyone agrees; there is no argument
Single straight boards placed between the corner-posts to close a large gap
We do not need

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the argument between רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה only matters for wider wells. Up to an 8-אמה well, the gap is 10 אמות or less, so the law is the same for both.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
With a well of eight (cubits wide),
everyone agrees, they do not argue,
that we do not need single boards.
phrases.notes: 8 + 2 + 2 = 12; minus 1 אמה for each corner-post = a 10-אמה gap.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: בְּבוֹר שְׁמוֹנֶה דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of the ברייתא to how the argument applies in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For an 8-אמה well, the gap between the corner-posts is 10 אמות, so even רבי מאיר requires no פשוטין.

steps.title: A twelve-אמה well: everyone requires single boards
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא continues his rule. For a בור twelve אמות wide, all opinions agree that פשוטין are required.
steps.simpleTranslation: For a well that is twelve אמות wide, everyone agrees that we need single boards.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives the other end of his rule. For a twelve-אמה well, both רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה require extra single boards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The enclosure must leave about two אמות on each side of the well for the cows. A twelve-אמה well therefore makes the enclosure about sixteen אמות wide. After the corner posts, the gap is about fourteen אמות, which is more than even רבי יהודה's limit of about thirteen and a third, so single boards are needed to close it.

keyTerms.meaning: A well or cistern
Everyone (all opinions agree)
Single straight boards placed between the corner posts to make the gaps smaller
We need / it is required

phrases.english: With a well of twelve (אמות),
phrases.notes: This is the opposite end from the eight-אמה case in step 8.

phrases.english: everyone does not disagree
phrases.notes: All opinions agree.

phrases.english: that we need single boards.
phrases.notes: The gap would be about fourteen אמות, which is too wide even for רבי יהודה.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּבוֹר שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב פפא's statement from step 8, giving the upper limit after the lower one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For a twelve-אמה well, all opinions require פשוטין.

steps.title: The disagreement applies only to wells between eight and twelve אמות
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא states where the מחלוקת actually matters: wells between eight and twelve אמות. רבי מאיר requires פשוטין there, and רבי יהודה does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Where do they disagree? For wells from eight to twelve אמות. רבי מאיר says we need single boards. רבי יהודה says we do not.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא finishes his rule by showing the range where רבי מאיר and רבי יהודה actually disagree in practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Within this range, the gap between the corner posts is more than ten אמות. That is too wide for רבי מאיר, whose limit is ten. רבי יהודה allows a gap of about thirteen and a third, so he does not need extra boards here.

keyTerms.meaning: Where they do disagree
From eight to twelve

steps.whatToRemember: At eight אמות, nobody needs פשוטין. At twelve אמות, everyone needs them. Between eight and twelve, רבי מאיר requires them and רבי יהודה does not.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי פְּלִיגִי — מִשְּׁמוֹנֶה עַד שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה.
phrases.english: Where they disagree is from eight to twelve.
phrases.notes: This is the range between the two agreed cases.

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Meir, we need single boards.
phrases.notes: His maximum gap is ten אמות.

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Yehuda, we do not need single boards.
phrases.notes: His maximum gap is about thirteen and a third אמות.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי מִשְּׁמוֹנֶה עַד שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב פפא's statement by defining the middle range where the opinions differ.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: For wells between eight and twelve אמות, רבי מאיר requires פשוטין and רבי יהודה does not.

steps.title: What did רב פפא add? We already learned this
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב פפא needed to say anything, since the ברייתא already gave both opinions' maximum gaps.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is רב פפא teaching us? We already learned this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב פפא's statement as unnecessary, since it seems to add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already said that רבי מאיר allows ten אמות and רבי יהודה allows about thirteen and a third. Anyone could work out רב פפא's ranges from those numbers. So the גמרא asks what new information he gave.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (What is new here?)

phrases.aramaic: וְרַב פָּפָּא מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן?
phrases.english: And Rav Pappa, what is he teaching us?
phrases.notes: The standard way of asking what a statement adds.

phrases.english: We already learned it!
phrases.notes: This refers to the ברייתא with the measurements of ten and thirteen and a third.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב פָּפָּא מַאי קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the statement given in steps 8 to 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's whole statement about eight, twelve, and the range in between
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A statement should teach something new. This one can be worked out directly from the ברייתא's numbers, so it seems unnecessary.

steps.title: רב פפא had not heard the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב פפא did not know the ברייתא. He reached the same conclusion on his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא had not heard the ברייתא, so he taught us what the ברייתא says.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The statement is not new to us, but רב פפא did not know the ברייתא and figured out the same rule himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא does not invent a new idea in רב פפא's words. It admits the statement matches the ברייתא and explains why he said it anyway. In effect, his reasoning ends up confirming the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: He had not heard it
Like (in agreement with) the ברייתא

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the גמרא found a new teaching in רב פפא's words. It agrees that nothing new was taught and only explains why he said it.
steps.whatToRemember: Sometimes the גמרא's answer is simply that an אמורא did not know an earlier source and reached the same conclusion independently.

phrases.aramaic: רַב פָּפָּא בָּרָיְיתָא לָא שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Pappa had not heard the baraita,
and he taught us as the baraita says.
phrases.notes: His own reasoning matched the ברייתא.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא בָּרָיְיתָא לָא שְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Admits the statement is not new and explains it historically (the speaker did not know the source)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב פפא's statement must contain some new teaching beyond the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: It adds nothing new. רב פפא simply did not know the ברייתא and reached the same conclusion himself.

steps.title: A memory aid for the coming questions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a סימן, a string of key words, to help remember a series of questions אביי asked רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Extended, more, in a mound, a barrier, a courtyard that dried up: this is a memory aid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up what comes next. Before the questions begin, it lists one key word from each question so a learner can remember their order.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word points to one upcoming question. 'אריך' (extended) points to the very first one, about widening the corner posts. This line has no legal content of its own. It is only an organizing tool.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory aid. A list of key words that helps you remember a series of teachings in order.

phrases.english: Extended, more, in a mound,
phrases.notes: Each word is a cue for one of אביי's upcoming questions.

phrases.english: a barrier, a courtyard that dried up: a memory aid.
phrases.notes: The word 'סימן' tells you this is a list of cues, not a ruling.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: Mnemonic / structural marker (no true argumentative function)
steps.triggerLanguage: אֲרִיךְ יוֹתֵר בְּתֵל חִיצַת חָצֵר שֶׁיָּבְשָׁה סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new unit after the discussion of רב פפא's ruling ended.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. It is a memory list for the series of questions אביי asked רבה.

steps.title: Can widening the corner posts replace adding single boards?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבה: if the corner posts are widened by the size of a single board, does that satisfy רבי מאיר?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked רבה: If someone made the corner posts longer by the size of a single board, what is the law according to רבי מאיר?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי asks a real question. When the gaps around the well are too wide, can a person make each corner post wider instead of putting separate single boards in the gaps?
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי מאיר, when the gaps are too wide, פשוטין (single boards) are needed. אביי wants to know whether the boards must stand on their own in the gap, or whether stretching the corner post by the same width works just as well. Either way, the gap shrinks by the same amount, so the question is whether the form matters.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him. Used for a real question one scholar asks another.
Corner posts. L-shaped pieces placed at the corners of the well.
He lengthened or extended (here: widened the arms of the corner posts).
By the measure of, the same size as.

phrases.english: Abaye asked Rabba:
If he extended the corner posts by the measure of single boards,
phrases.notes: He widened each arm of the corner post by about one אמה, the width of a single board.

phrases.english: according to Rabbi Meir, what is the law?
phrases.notes: רבי מאיר is the one who requires פשוטין, so the question is asked on his view.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the first question listed in the סימן ('אריך').
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, for רבי מאיר, widening the corner posts by a board's width does the same job as adding a separate single board.

steps.title: רבה brings the משנה's words as proof
steps.stepSummary: רבה cites the משנה, 'provided that he increases the boards,' and suggests it means widening the corner posts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: You already learned it: 'Provided that he increases the boards.' Doesn't this mean that he extends the corner posts?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers by pointing to a phrase in the משנה. He suggests that 'increase the boards' means making the corner posts bigger, which would mean widening them does work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה allows the boards to be placed farther from the well, 'provided that he increases the boards.' רבה reads 'increase' as 'make wider,' so widening the corner posts would be explicitly allowed. That would answer אביי's question with a yes.

keyTerms.meaning: You have already learned it. Meaning: the answer is already in a source you know.
Provided that he increases the boards. The key phrase from the משנה.
Doesn't it mean...? A way of suggesting a reading as proof.

phrases.english: He said to him: You learned it:
"Provided that he increases the boards."
phrases.notes: Quoted from the משנה about boards around wells.

phrases.english: Doesn't this mean that he extends the corner posts?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבה tries to answer אביי's question from the משנה.
steps.raayaObject: That widening the corner posts is valid according to רבי מאיר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's phrase 'ובלבד שירבה בפסין', read as making the boards bigger.

steps.title: אביי: it may mean adding more boards
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects the proof: the phrase can mean adding more single boards, not widening the posts.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It means that he adds more and makes single boards.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי pushes back. He says the משנה's phrase could just as easily mean 'put in more single boards,' so it does not prove anything about widening the corner posts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'increase the boards' means increase their number, the משנה only teaches what we already knew: add פשוטין. Then the case of widening the corner posts is not addressed at all, so רבה's proof fails in this version. Step 21 later settles the question from the wording.

keyTerms.meaning: That he adds more, increases the number.
And makes.

phrases.english: No, it means that he adds more and makes single boards.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבה's reading of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not decide the law either way.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The phrase is ambiguous: 'increase' can mean more boards, not wider posts.

steps.title: The wording doesn't fit 'more boards'
steps.stepSummary: The challenge: if the משנה meant more boards, it should have said 'עד שירבה פסין' without the letter ב.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, this phrase 'provided that he increases in the boards' should have said 'until he increases the boards'!
steps.whatsHappening: The challenge is aimed at אביי's reading. The exact wording 'בפסין' (in the boards) sounds like making the boards themselves bigger, not adding more of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The little letter ב in 'בפסין' suggests growth inside the boards, which means widening. If the meaning were 'more boards,' the natural wording would be 'שירבה פסין.' So the wording seems to support רבה's reading.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. Opens a challenge based on what was just said.
It should have said. Points out that the wording seems wrong for the suggested reading.

phrases.english: If so, this "provided that he increases in the boards"
phrases.notes: Focus on the letter ב in 'בפסין'.

phrases.english: it should have said "until he increases the boards"!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, הַאי וּבִלְבַד שֶׁיַּרְבֶּה בְּפַסִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's rejection from the exact wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading that the משנה means adding more single boards.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wording 'בפסין' implies enlarging the boards themselves. A number increase would be written 'פסין' without the ב.

steps.title: Read the words as 'more boards'
steps.stepSummary: The answer: simply read the משנה as 'עד שירבה פסין', meaning more boards.
steps.simpleTranslation: Read it as: 'until he increases the boards.'
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is that we should not lean too hard on the wording. Just read the משנה as if it said 'increase the boards,' meaning add more of them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ב is not treated as decisive. The phrase is understood as 'add more boards,' so אביי's rejection stands and the משנה still gives no proof about widening the corner posts.

phrases.english: Read: "until he increases the boards."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the wording challenge and keeps אביי's rejection standing.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading adjustment (the wording is not precise enough to prove anything)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ב in 'בפסין' proves the משנה means widening the boards.
steps.terutzMaskana: Read the phrase as 'more boards'. In this version the proof fails. Step 21 later settles the question from the wording.

steps.title: Second version: רבה reads the משנה as 'more boards'
steps.stepSummary: In another version, רבה cites the same משנה but reads it as adding more single boards, which would mean widening is not enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רבה said to him: You learned it: 'Provided that he increases the boards.' Doesn't this mean that he adds more and makes single boards?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of the same conversation. Here רבה uses the משנה to prove the opposite: real single boards are needed, so widening the corner posts does not help.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Same source, opposite proof. If 'increase the boards' means adding more boards, then the משנה requires separate פשוטין, and widening the corner posts would not count for רבי מאיר.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two versions. In the first, רבה reads the משנה as 'widen the posts.' In the second, he reads it as 'add more boards.' In both versions אביי shows the phrase can be read the other way.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
He said to him: You learned it:
"Provided that he increases the boards."
Doesn't this mean that he adds more and makes single boards?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the exchange in a different version with the proof reversed.
steps.raayaObject: That widening the corner posts is not enough according to רבי מאיר. Real single boards are required.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The same משנה phrase, read as increasing the number of boards.

steps.title: אביי: it may mean widening the posts
steps.stepSummary: אביי rejects again: the phrase can mean widening the corner posts, so there is no proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It means that he extends the corner posts.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the second version by saying the משנה might mean widening the corner posts. So, once again, nothing is proven.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ב in 'בפסין' actually helps אביי's alternate reading, so no wording challenge follows. The next step builds on this exact point and declares this reading the more reasonable one.

keyTerms.meaning: That he extends or widens.

steps.whatToRemember: אביי asked whether, for רבי מאיר, widening the corner posts by a board's width can replace separate single boards. In both versions רבה's proof from 'ובלבד שירבה בפסין' is rejected. The next step decides that the wording favors 'widen the posts.'

phrases.english: No, it means that he extends the corner posts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof given in the second version.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from the משנה. The law itself is not decided.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The phrase can equally mean widening the corner posts.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In this version אביי reads the משנה as widening the corner posts. Step 21 accepts this reading as the correct one.

steps.title: The wording of the משנה supports the widening reading
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says it makes sense that the corner posts may be widened. The proof is the משנה's phrase "שֶׁיַּרְבֶּה בְּפַסִּין", and the matter is settled.
steps.simpleTranslation: So too it is reasonable, since the משנה teaches: 'provided that he increases with the boards.' Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the back-and-forth from the last few steps. It decides that the משנה's wording supports the version where widening the corner posts is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 20, אביי said the phrase could mean widening the corner posts. Now the גמרא agrees and calls this the more reasonable reading. The letter ב in "בְּפַסִּין" suggests adding width to the existing posts, not adding new separate boards.

keyTerms.meaning: So too it is logical. A formula that brings support for the view just stated.
From the fact that it teaches
Learn from it. The point is accepted.
Boards or posts set up around a well

steps.whatToRemember: Conclusion so far: you may make the corner posts wider. You do not have to add separate single boards. The proof is the ב in "בְּפַסִּין".

phrases.english: So too it is reasonable,
from the fact that it teaches:
'provided that he increases with the boards.'
phrases.notes: The ב suggests adding width to the posts themselves.

phrases.english: Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts אביי's reading from step 20 and supports it from the wording of the משנה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The משנה's phrase "שֶׁיַּרְבֶּה בְּפַסִּין" supports widening the existing corner posts.

steps.title: אביי's question: single boards or wider corner posts for big gaps
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבה what to do according to רבי יהודה when a gap is more than 13⅓ אמות. Do you add single boards, or widen the corner posts?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked רבה: If the gap is more than thirteen and a third אמות, what is the law according to רבי יהודה? Does he put in single boards, or does he lengthen the double corner posts?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי opens a new question. It is about how to close a gap that is too large, according to רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה allows gaps of up to 13⅓ אמות between the posts. If the gap is bigger, it must be made smaller. There are two possible ways: add single boards (פשוטין) in the middle, or widen the L-shaped corner posts (דיומדין) so the gap shrinks.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him. A real question, not an attack.
Single, flat boards
Double corner posts, shaped like an L
He lengthens or widens
Thirteen and a third אמות. רבי יהודה's largest allowed gap.

phrases.english: Abaye asked of Rabba:
If the gap is more than thirteen and a third cubits,
according to Rabbi Yehuda, what is the law?
Does he make single boards,
or does he lengthen the double corner posts?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the settled reading of the משנה to a new question about רבי יהודה's view.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: According to רבי יהודה, when a gap is more than 13⅓ אמות, is it fixed by adding single boards or by widening the corner posts?

steps.title: רבה quotes a ברייתא on how close and how far the posts may be
steps.stepSummary: רבה says the answer is already found in a ברייתא. The posts may be as close as a cow's head and most of its body, and as far as a כור or even two כורים of area.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You already learned it. How close may they be? The length of the head and most of the body of a cow. And how far may they be? Even a כור of area, and even two כורים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה begins his answer by quoting a ברייתא. This step is the first part of it, the view of the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The minimum distance lets a cow stand inside with its head and most of its body and drink. The חכמים put no real limit on how far out the enclosure can go, even a huge area, as long as the gaps are kept within the limit. רבה will use this ברייתא, together with רבי יהודה's view in the next step, to answer אביי.

keyTerms.meaning: You have already learned it
Close (to the well)
Far (from the well)
A cow's head and most of its body
A large measure of area: the land needed to plant a כור of seed

phrases.english: He said to him: You have learned it.
How close may they be?
The length of the head and most of the body of a cow.
And how far may they be?
Even a kor, and even two kor.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts רבה's answer to אביי's question by quoting a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבה says the answer is in a ברייתא about how close and how far the posts may be. From רבי יהודה's limit of בית סאתים, he infers that for רבי יהודה one widens the corner posts. Step 27 challenges this inference.

steps.title: רבי יהודה limits the enclosure to בית סאתים
steps.stepSummary: In the ברייתא, רבי יהודה says that up to בית סאתים is permitted, and more than בית סאתים is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: An area of בית סאתים is permitted. More than בית סאתים is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא goes on with רבי יהודה's view. He disagrees with the חכמים and puts a limit on the size of the enclosed area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים allowed even a כור or two כורים. רבי יהודה allows only up to בית סאתים, the size of the courtyard of the משכן. This limit is the key to answering אביי's question about how to close large gaps.

keyTerms.meaning: An area for planting two סאה of seed: 5,000 square אמות, like the courtyard of the משכן
Permitted
Forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two arguments. In the משנה, רבי יהודה is the lenient one about the size of the gaps (13⅓ אמות). Here he is the strict one about the total area (only בית סאתים).

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
An area of two beit se'a is permitted;
more than two beit se'a is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: בֵּית סָאתַיִם מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי יהודה's opposing view inside the same ברייתא that רבה quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, the enclosure around the well may be at most בית סאתים.

steps.title: The חכמים challenge רבי יהודה from pens and courtyards
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask רבי יהודה a question. Doesn't he agree that a pen, a stable, a backyard, or a courtyard is permitted even if it is five or ten כורים in size?
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to רבי יהודה: Don't you agree that a pen, a stable, a backyard, and a courtyard are permitted, even if the area is five כורים or even ten כורים?
steps.whatsHappening: Still inside the ברייתא, the חכמים push back against רבי יהודה's limit. They point to other enclosures where even he allows a very large area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים argue that size should not matter. Enclosed areas like a דיר, סהר, מוקצה, and חצר are permitted no matter how big they are. So why should the area around the well be limited to בית סאתים? The question is phrased as asking for agreement, but it works as a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't you agree? An argument from something he already accepts.
A pen for animals
A stable or enclosure for animals
A backyard storage area behind houses
Courtyard

phrases.english: They said to Rabbi Yehuda:
Do you not agree
regarding a pen, a stable, a backyard, and a courtyard,
that even one of five kor
and even one of ten kor is permitted?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה: אִי אַתָּה מוֹדֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The חכמים challenge רבי יהודה's limit of בית סאתים, inside the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's rule that the area around the well may not be more than בית סאתים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Other enclosures (pen, stable, backyard, courtyard) are permitted at any size, even according to רבי יהודה. So limiting the well enclosure seems inconsistent.

steps.title: A wall is different from posts
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה answers the חכמים: a courtyard has a real מחיצה, but the area around a well only has פסין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said to them: This one (the courtyard) is a real wall, but these (around the well) are only posts.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה answers the challenge from Step 25. He explains why a big courtyard is allowed while a big area around a well is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים argued that if a huge courtyard is permitted, a huge area around a well should be permitted too. רבי יהודה says the cases are not the same. A courtyard is closed in by a real wall, but the well area is closed in only by posts, which are a weaker kind of enclosure. So the posts are limited to בית סאתים.

keyTerms.meaning: A real partition or wall
Upright posts or boards placed around a well
He said to them

steps.whyThisMatters: This one line sets up the whole next exchange. The גמרא will now test whether this wording fits רבה's understanding of the ברייתא.

phrases.english: He (רבי יהודה) said to them:
This is a partition, but these are posts.
phrases.notes: 'This' is the courtyard wall; 'these' are the posts around the well.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: זוֹ מְחִיצָה, וְאֵלּוּ פַּסִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the חכמים' challenge from Step 25
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction between cases (a real wall versus posts)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A courtyard and the area around a well are the same, so both should be allowed at any size.
steps.terutzMaskana: A courtyard has a real wall, so any size works. A well only has posts, so it is limited to בית סאתים.

steps.title: The wording seems to go against רבה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the posts could be widened into something like a full wall, רבי יהודה should have said 'both are partitions.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it is so (as רבה understood), he should have said: 'This is a partition and that is also a partition!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה's use of this ברייתא. It says the wording 'these are posts' does not fit his reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבה's reading, the posts around the well are extended until they work like a real wall. If so, the well area would be just like a courtyard. Then רבי יהודה should have said both are partitions, not 'this is a wall and these are posts.'

keyTerms.meaning: And if it is so (if your claim were true)
He should have said

phrases.english: And if it is so (as רבה said),
'This is a partition and that is also a partition'
he should have said!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִם אִיתָא, זוֹ מְחִיצָה וְזוֹ הִיא מְחִיצָה מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רבי יהודה's wording from Step 26 to challenge רבה's reading of the ברייתא from Step 23
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If extended posts become a real partition, רבי יהודה would not have contrasted 'wall' with 'posts.'

steps.title: Two different rules for gaps
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי יהודה meant a wall has wall rules, with gaps up to ten אמות, while posts have post rules, with gaps up to 13⅓ אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he meant: This one follows the rules of a partition, so its gaps may be up to ten אמות. These follow the rules of posts, so their gaps may be up to thirteen and a third אמות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains that רבי יהודה was pointing to the different rules for gaps, not saying posts can never act as an enclosure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Wall' and 'posts' here mean two legal systems. A wall only allows gaps up to ten אמות. Posts allow larger gaps, up to 13⅓ אמות. Because posts are a weaker enclosure, רבי יהודה limits them to בית סאתים. So the wording does not prove anything about אביי's question, and the issue stays open.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he meant
The legal rules of a partition
Gaps or breaches in an enclosure
A cubit, a unit of length

steps.whatToRemember: A real מחיצה allows gaps of up to ten אמות. פסין around a well allow gaps of up to 13⅓ אמות. For רבי יהודה, this weaker enclosure is limited to בית סאתים.
steps.confusionAlert: 'These are posts' does not mean the posts fail to enclose. It means they follow a different, more lenient set of rules about gaps.

phrases.english: This is what he meant:
This one has the rules of a partition —
so its gaps may be up to ten (אמות),
and these have the rules of posts —
so their gaps may be up to thirteen and a third אמות.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי קָאָמַר: זוֹ תּוֹרַת מְחִיצָה עָלֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 27 by reinterpreting רבי יהודה's words
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of wording (two sets of rules for gaps)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'These are posts' means posts cannot work like a partition.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Wall' and 'posts' refer to different rules for gaps: ten אמות versus 13⅓ אמות.

steps.title: Can a mound count as a corner post?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבה whether a mound that rises ten טפחים within four אמות can serve as a דיומד (corner post).
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked רבה: A mound that rises ten טפחים within four אמות — is it treated as a corner post, or not?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי opens a new question. He asks whether a natural slope can take the place of a built corner post around a well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slope that rises ten טפחים within four אמות is steep enough to count as a מחיצה in other places. The question is whether it can also fill the specific role of a דיומד. A דיומד is a corner piece made of two boards set at an angle.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked him (a question seeking information)
A mound that rises upward gradually
A double post: a corner piece made of two boards set at an angle
Is judged or treated as

phrases.english: אביי asked רבה:
A mound that rises ten (טפחים)
within (a span of) four (אמות),
is it treated as a double post
or is it not treated as a double post?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question after the previous discussion ends
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a natural mound rising ten טפחים within four אמות can serve as a דיומד.

steps.title: רבה quotes a ברייתא: a square stone can count as a corner post
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers אביי from a ברייתא. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר rules that a square stone counts as a דיומד if we can picture an L-shape of one אמה by one אמה inside it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: You have already learned this. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: If a square stone was there, we look at it this way. If you could picture it divided so that it has one אמה in this direction and one אמה in that direction, it counts as a דיומד. If not, it does not count as a דיומד.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה begins his answer to אביי's question about the mound. He tells אביי the answer is already in a ברייתא, and he quotes its first opinion, which is about a square stone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A דיומד is normally two boards, each one אמה wide, joined at a corner like an L. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says a solid square stone also works. We use רואין: we picture the extra stone removed and ask whether an L of one אמה by one אמה would be left. This shows a דיומד does not have to be built from boards. Any natural object of the right size and shape can count.

keyTerms.meaning: You have already learned it (in a ברייתא)
A square stone
We view it as if: we picture the object changed in our minds
A corner post shaped like an L, with one אמה in each direction
It is treated as / it counts as

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody actually cuts the stone. רואין means we only picture the change in our minds. The stone stays as it is and still counts.

phrases.english: He (Rabba) said to him: You have learned it:
phrases.notes: רבה points to a ברייתא that already answers the question.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
If a square stone was there,
we view it: wherever, if it were divided,
phrases.notes: We picture the stone cut into an L-shape.

it counts as a double (corner) post,

phrases.english: and if not, it does not count as a double post.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from step 29 by citing a ברייתא.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A ברייתא already teaches that a stone can be a דיומד if, viewed as if divided, it has one אמה in each direction.

steps.title: A round stone also counts if it is pictured as trimmed and then divided
steps.stepSummary: רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה rules that even a round stone counts as a דיומד. We picture it first trimmed into a square and then cut into an L-shape.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ישמעאל, the son of רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה, says: If a round stone was there, we look at it this way. If you could picture it chiseled into a square and then divided so that it has one אמה this way and one אמה that way, it counts as a דיומד. If not, it does not count as a דיומד.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה continues quoting the ברייתא with a second opinion. This opinion allows even a round stone, and it is the part that really answers the question about a mound.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A round stone needs two mental steps. First we picture it chiseled into a square, and then we picture that square divided into an L. A mound is uneven and rounded like such a stone, so according to this opinion a mound can also count as a דיומד.

keyTerms.meaning: A round stone
It would be chiseled (trimmed into a square)
It would be divided (into an L-shape)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is what proves the mound case. A mound, like a round stone, needs more than one act of 'picturing' to become a proper דיומד.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, says:
If a round stone was there,
we view it: wherever, if it were chiseled and then divided,
phrases.notes: Two mental steps: first trim it into a square, then cut it into an L.

phrases.aramaic: וְיֵשׁ בָּהּ אַמָּה לְכָאן וְאַמָּה לְכָאן —
phrases.english: it would have a cubit this way and a cubit that way,
it counts as a double post,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם לָאו — אֵינוֹ נִידּוֹן מִשּׁוּם דְּיוֹמָד.
phrases.english: and if not, it does not count as a double post.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן בְּרוֹקָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא with a broader opinion that covers round objects.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a mound can serve as a דיומד.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling in the ברייתא by רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה about a round stone.

steps.title: What exactly do the two תנאים disagree about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the underlying point of disagreement between the two opinions in the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: About what do they disagree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the real argument between the two תנאים is. This question sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At first glance, one opinion speaks about a square stone and the other about a round one. The גמרא wants to know the principle behind the difference, and why one Sage would not accept the round stone.

keyTerms.meaning: About what do they disagree?

phrases.english: With regard to what do they disagree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the principle behind the two opinions just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying principle that divides רבי שמעון בן אלעזר and רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה.

steps.title: They disagree whether we may picture changes once or twice
steps.stepSummary: One Sage allows only one act of רואין. The other allows even two.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds that we use 'we view it as if' once, but we do not use it twice. The other Sage holds that we use 'we view it as if' even twice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the disagreement. It is about how many imagined changes we are allowed to make to an object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר allows only one imagined change: dividing a square stone into an L. A round stone would need two changes (trimming and then dividing), so he does not accept it. רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה allows two imagined changes, so a round stone, and also a mound, can count.

keyTerms.meaning: One Sage holds
One act of 'we view it as if'
Two acts of 'we view it as if'
We say / we apply

steps.whatToRemember: The argument is over one רואין versus two. A square stone needs one imagined change, and a round stone needs two. A mound is like a round stone, so it works according to the opinion that accepts two רואין.

phrases.english: One Sage holds: we say 'we view' once,
phrases.notes: This is רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.

phrases.english: but we do not say 'we view' twice,

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: אֲפִילּוּ תְּרֵי רוֹאִין נָמֵי אָמְרִינַן.
phrases.english: and the other Sage holds: even 'we view' twice we also say.
phrases.notes: This is רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 32.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They disagree whether רואין can be applied twice (trimming and dividing) or only once (dividing).

steps.title: Can a fence of reeds placed close together count as a corner post?
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבה a new question. Does a row of reeds, each less than three טפחים from the next, count as a דיומד?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי asked רבה: A fence of reeds, where each reed is less than three טפחים from the next, does it count as a דיומד or not?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי opens a new question about a different kind of material. Here the question is about reeds with small gaps between them instead of one solid object.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, gaps of less than three טפחים are treated as closed because of the rule of לבוד. אביי asks whether that rule can join separate reeds into a solid corner post. The question is whether the reeds can count as one solid דיומד through לבוד.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked of him (introduces a question)
A fence (barrier) of reeds
Less than three טפחים apart
The rule that a gap of less than three טפחים is treated as closed

phrases.english: Abaye asked of Rabba:
A barrier of reeds,
each reed less than three handbreadths from the next,
phrases.notes: This is close enough to apply the rule of לבוד.

phrases.english: does it count as a double post or not?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the mound question is answered, אביי asks a new related question about reeds.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether reeds joined only by לבוד can be treated as a solid דיומד.

steps.title: רבה answers from a ברייתא about a barrier of reeds
steps.stepSummary: רבה cites a ברייתא that says a tree, a fence, or a barrier of reeds counts as a דיומד. He suggests that the 'barrier of reeds' means a row of reeds each less than three טפחים apart.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: You already learned this in a ברייתא. 'If there was a tree there, or a fence, or a barrier of reeds, it is treated as a דיומד.' Doesn't this mean reeds standing one by one, each less than three טפחים from the next?
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers אביי's question by quoting a ברייתא. He argues that the ברייתא's 'barrier of reeds' is exactly the case אביי asked about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא lists three things that work as a דיומד. רבה reads the third one, חיצת הקנים, as a row of reeds with small gaps. Because of the rule of לבוד, gaps under three טפחים count as closed. If this reading is right, אביי's question is answered: yes, such a row counts.

keyTerms.meaning: You (pl.) already learned it — introduces a proof from a ברייתא
A barrier or partition made of reeds
A double post: an L-shaped corner piece used for the well enclosure
Is it not…? — introduces a suggested reading of a source
Reed after reed, each less than three טפחים apart

steps.confusionAlert: The proof depends on the words 'מאי לאו' ('Isn't it…?'). This is only a suggested reading of the ברייתא, and the very next step will challenge it.

phrases.english: He (Rabba) said to him: You have learned it:
phrases.notes: רבה is answering אביי here.

phrases.english: If there was a tree there or a fence
or a barrier of reeds
it is treated as a double post.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו, קָנֶה קָנֶה פָּחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה?
phrases.english: Is it not referring to reed after reed, each less than three handbreadths apart?
phrases.notes: This is how רבה suggests reading it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question from Step 34
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A row of reeds less than three טפחים apart counts as a דיומד, based on the ברייתא's חיצת הקנים
steps.raayaObject: Whether a row of spaced reeds counts as a דיומד
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא: היה שם אילן או גדר או חיצת הקנים נידון משום דיומד

steps.title: Maybe the ברייתא means a dense thicket of reeds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבה's reading. The ברייתא might mean a thick cluster of reeds, not a spaced row.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It might mean a thicket of reeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. It says the ברייתא's 'barrier of reeds' could mean a solid, dense clump of reeds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thicket of reeds grows so tightly that it works like one solid post. If that is what the ברייתא means, it says nothing about reeds with gaps between them. So אביי's question would remain open.

keyTerms.meaning: A thicket or dense cluster of reeds growing close together

phrases.english: No, it refers to a thicket of reeds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in Step 35 by offering another reading of the ברייתא
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the reading of חיצת הקנים as spaced reeds, not the ברייתא itself
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא could be talking about a dense thicket, so it does not prove anything about spaced reeds

steps.title: A thicket of reeds would be the same as a tree
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the pushback. A thicket of reeds is basically a tree, so the ברייתא would be repeating itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, it is the same as a tree!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading from Step 36. If the ברייתא meant a solid thicket, that case is already covered by 'tree'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ברייתא normally does not list the same kind of case twice. A thicket and a tree are both solid, growing objects. So listing 'barrier of reeds' separately suggests it means something different, like a spaced row.

keyTerms.meaning: If so — introduces a challenge based on the previous claim
That is the same as…
Tree

phrases.english: If so, that is the same as a tree!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the alternate reading offered in Step 36
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of חיצת הקנים as a thicket of reeds
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A thicket is the same as a tree, and the ברייתא would not list the same case twice

steps.title: Either reading leaves a doubled case, so the ברייתא proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that spaced reeds would just be a fence. So either way the ברייתא lists two kinds of the same thing, and 'two kinds of tree' is just as acceptable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what else would you say? That it means reed after reed, each less than three טפחים apart? That is the same as a fence! You would have to say the ברייתא lists two kinds of fence. Here too, it lists two kinds of tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the 'thicket' reading. It shows that the opposite reading has the very same problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under לבוד, a row of reeds with small gaps already counts as a fence. So רבה's reading also makes the ברייתא repeat itself. Since a repeat cannot be avoided either way, the ברייתא may be listing two types of tree. As a result, the proof for אביי's question falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: But what then? — turns the challenge back on the other reading
Fence
Two types or varieties
Here too

steps.whatToRemember: In this first version, the ברייתא does not settle whether a row of spaced reeds counts as a דיומד. Both readings of חיצת הקנים repeat a case already in the list ('fence' or 'tree').
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not claiming that spaced reeds are invalid. It only shows that the ברייתא cannot prove they are valid.

phrases.english: But rather, what?

phrases.aramaic: קָנֶה קָנֶה פָּחוֹת מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה — הַיְינוּ גָּדֵר!
phrases.english: Reed after reed less than three handbreadths apart — that is the same as a fence!
Rather, what must you say?
That it teaches two types of fence?
Here too, it teaches two types of tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 37 and restores the דחיה of Step 36
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turning the objection back on the other reading (repetition is unavoidable either way)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Reading חיצת הקנים as a thicket makes the ברייתא repeat 'tree'
steps.terutzMaskana: The other reading repeats 'fence', so a repeat is acceptable. The ברייתא may list two kinds of tree, and the proof falls away

steps.title: Second version: the question was about a thicket of reeds
steps.stepSummary: Some report the exchange differently. In their version, אביי asked רבה whether a dense thicket of reeds counts as a דיומד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: It was a thicket of reeds that he asked about. What is the law of a thicket of reeds?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the whole discussion. This line restates אביי's question and sets up רבה's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, אביי's doubt is about a solid cluster of reeds, not a spaced row. He may have been unsure because the reeds are thin, separate stalks even though they grow close together.

keyTerms.meaning: He was asking about this; it was his question

phrases.english: There are those who say:
It was about a thicket of reeds that he asked.
What is the law of a thicket of reeds?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the exchange with a different version of אביי's question
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a dense thicket of reeds counts as a דיומד

steps.title: רבה proves from the ברייתא that a thicket of reeds counts
steps.stepSummary: רבה cites the same ברייתא. He reads 'barrier of reeds' as a thicket, so a thicket counts as a דיומד.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: You already learned this. 'If there was a fence there, or a tree, or a barrier of reeds, it is treated as a דיומד.' Doesn't this mean a thicket of reeds?
steps.whatsHappening: In the second version, רבה answers אביי with the same ברייתא. This time the ברייתא is read as being about a thicket.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the 'barrier of reeds' is read exactly as the pushback in Step 36 read it, a dense thicket. This is only a suggested reading (מאי לאו). The next step rejects it, just as the first version's proof was rejected.
steps.whatToRemember: In the second version, אביי's question is about a dense thicket of reeds. רבה tries to prove from the ברייתא that it counts, and steps 41–43 challenge that proof the same way the first version's proof was challenged.
steps.whyThisMatters: The same ברייתא is brought as proof for opposite cases, depending on which question was asked. In each version the proof is rejected because חיצת הקנים can be read either way.

phrases.english: He said to him: You have learned it:
If there was a fence there or a tree
or a barrier of reeds
it is treated as a double post.
Is it not referring to a thicket of reeds?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of the second version in Step 39
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A thicket of reeds counts as a דיומד, based on the ברייתא's חיצת הקנים
steps.raayaObject: Whether a thicket of reeds counts as a דיומד
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא: היה שם גדר או אילן או חיצת הקנים נידון משום דיומד
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In the איכא דאמרי version, רבה proposes that the ברייתא's חיצת הקנים means a thicket. The proposal is challenged in steps 41–43.

steps.title: Maybe the barrier is spaced reeds, not a thicket
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבה's proof. The ברייתא's 'barrier of reeds' could mean single reeds standing less than three טפחים apart, not a dense thicket.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It may mean reed after reed, each less than three handbreadths from the next.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבה's proof from the ברייתא. It offers another way to read 'barrier of reeds.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה needed the ברייתא to be talking about a thicket. The גמרא says it could instead mean a row of separate reeds with gaps smaller than three טפחים. Gaps that small are treated as closed, so such a row works as a wall. If that is what the ברייתא means, it proves nothing about a thicket.

keyTerms.meaning: No. Opens a rejection of the previous proof.
Reed by reed: individual reeds standing one after another.
Less than three טפחים, the gap size that is treated as closed (לבוד).

steps.confusionAlert: This mirrors step 36, but it is reversed. There the pushback was 'it means a thicket.' Here, in the second version, the pushback is 'it means spaced reeds.'

phrases.english: No,
it means reed after reed, each less than three handbreadths apart.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבה's proof from step 40 by offering a different reading of the ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not prove that a thicket fails to count.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: 'Barrier of reeds' does not have to mean a thicket. It could mean spaced reeds within three טפחים.

steps.title: Then it is just a fence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects to the pushback. Spaced reeds working as a wall are simply a fence, which the ברייתא already lists.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, that is the same as a fence!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new reading from step 41. It says that reading would make the ברייתא repeat itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא already names a fence (גדר) as a valid barrier. A row of reeds with tiny gaps is really just a kind of fence. So listing 'barrier of reeds' separately would add nothing, which suggests it must mean something else, such as a thicket.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. Introduces a problem that follows from what was just said.
That is the same as. Points out a repetition.
Fence, already listed in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: If so,
it is the same as a fence!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the spaced-reeds reading proposed in step 41.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'barrier of reeds' means spaced reeds less than three טפחים apart.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reading makes the ברייתא repeat 'fence,' which it already listed.

steps.title: A thicket would just be a tree, so repetition is unavoidable
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the thicket reading has the same problem, since a thicket is basically a tree. It then begins to say what we are forced to conclude.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what then? A thicket of reeds is the same as a tree! Rather, what must you say is...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the spaced-reeds reading by showing that the other reading repeats too. It then starts to state the conclusion, which finishes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'barrier of reeds' meant a thicket, it would repeat 'tree,' which the ברייתא also lists. So either reading leaves the ברייתא with two items of the same kind. Since repetition happens either way, the objection in step 42 cannot prove that the ברייתא means a thicket.

keyTerms.meaning: But what then? Turns the challenge back on the other reading.
A thicket, or dense cluster, of reeds.
Tree, already listed in the ברייתא.
You must say. Introduces the forced conclusion.

steps.whyThisMatters: This returns the argument to a standoff. Neither reading avoids repetition, so the ברייתא no longer proves that a thicket counts as a דיומד.

phrases.english: But what then?
Would it be a thicket of reeds?
That is the same as a tree!
Rather, what must you say is...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 42 by showing that the thicket reading also repeats. It then begins the forced conclusion, which continues on the next amud.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Parity: the same objection applies to the other side, so it cannot decide between them.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The repetition of 'fence' proves that the ברייתא means a thicket.
